Mine production rose last year for the first time since 2003 while scrap recovery jumped by more than 25% for the second consecutive year. Meanwhile, jewellery fabrication collapsed by one-fifth, and not just because of the economic downturn. Gold is increasingly being priced out of many of its erstwhile important jewellery markets. Recent prices have lifted the incentive to thrift in industrial uses too. So long as investment interest stays strong, higher production and lower fabrication may not undermine quotations. However, it is hard to believe that the switch to safe-haven investment will ever again be as strong as in 2009. Coat-tailing gold, silver prices have also increased sharply since late 2008, but the supply-side response has been even sharper here as a plethora of new mines gear up for first production in Latin America. And ETFs have broadened the investor base for palladium and platinum too, although physical demand there continues to be held back by the malaise in the automotive sector. CRU’s Precious Metal Quarterly assesses the impact that current prices will have on the fundamentals of gold, silver, platinum and palladium supply and demand, and iterates back to whether these prices are sustainable given likely drivers of investment activity.
